title: Differentiation
description: First principles, derivative rules (power, product, quotient, chain), standard derivatives, tangents and normals, stationary points, second derivative test, concavity, points of inflection, related rates, and optimisation.

notes.heading: First Principles and Derivative Rules
notes.body:
Differentiation lets us find the gradient of a curve at any point. It is one of the most powerful tools in calculus.

📌 Definition — Derivative from First Principles
The derivative of $f(x)$ is the limit of the gradient of a chord as the chord shrinks to a point:
    $$f'(x) = \lim_{h 	o 0} \dfrac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$
This gives the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $x$.

🔑 The Power Rule
For any rational power $n$:
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^n) = n x^{n-1}$$
• If $f(x) = a x^n$, then $f'(x) = a n x^{n-1}$
• The derivative of a constant is zero
• The derivative of $x$ is $1$

💡 Worked Example — Power Rule
Differentiate $f(x) = 2x^3 + \dfrac{4}{x}$ for $x > 0$.

  Step 1: Rewrite using negative powers
    $$f(x) = 2x^3 + 4x^{-1}$$

  Step 2: Differentiate term by term
    $$f'(x) = 2 \cdot 3x^2 + 4 \cdot (-1)x^{-2}$$
    $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 4x^{-2}$$

  Step 3: Write with fractions
    $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - \dfrac{4}{x^2}$$

  Step 4: Find the gradient at $x = 4$
    $$f'(4) = 6(16) - \dfrac{4}{16} = 96 - 0.25 = 95.75$$

🔑 Product Rule
If $y = u v$ where $u$ and $v$ are both functions of $x$:
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u \dfrac{dv}{dx} + v \dfrac{du}{dx}$$
    or in dash notation: $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$

🔑 Quotient Rule
If $y = \dfrac{u}{v}$ where $u$ and $v$ are both functions of $x$:
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{v \dfrac{du}{dx} - u \dfrac{dv}{dx}}{v^2}$$
    or in dash notation: $\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)' = \dfrac{vu' - uv'}{v^2}$

💡 Worked Example — Product and Quotient Rules
a) Find the derivative of $y = e^x \sin x$
    Let $u = e^x \rightarrow u' = e^x$
    Let $v = \sin x \rightarrow v' = \cos x$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = u v' + v u' = e^x \cos x + \sin x \cdot e^x$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^x(\cos x + \sin x)$$

b) Differentiate $f(x) = \dfrac{2x + 1}{x - 3}$
    Let $u = 2x + 1 \rightarrow u' = 2$
    Let $v = x - 3 \rightarrow v' = 1$
    $$f'(x) = \dfrac{v u' - u v'}{v^2}$$
    $$f'(x) = \dfrac{(x - 3) \cdot 2 - (2x + 1) \cdot 1}{(x - 3)^2}$$
    $$f'(x) = \dfrac{2x - 6 - 2x - 1}{(x - 3)^2}$$
    $$f'(x) = \dfrac{-7}{(x - 3)^2}$$

🔑 Chain Rule
For a composite function $y = f(g(x))$:
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$$
    or if $y = f(u)$ where $u = g(x)$:
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$$

Think of it as "differentiate the outside, leave the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside."

💡 Worked Example — Chain Rule
Find the derivative of $y = (x^2 - 5x + 7)^7$.

  Step 1: Identify the inner and outer functions
    Inside: $u = x^2 - 5x + 7$
    Outside: $y = u^7$

  Step 2: Differentiate each part
    $$\dfrac{dy}{du} = 7u^6$$
    $$\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2x - 5$$

  Step 3: Apply the chain rule
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 7u^6 \cdot (2x - 5)$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 7(x^2 - 5x + 7)^6 \cdot (2x - 5)$$

🔑 Standard Derivatives (in formula booklet)
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln x) = \dfrac{1}{x} \quad (x > 0)$$

For composite versions, multiply by the derivative of the inner function:
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin(ax + b)) = a \cos(ax + b)$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{ax + b}) = a e^{ax + b}$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln(ax + b)) = \dfrac{a}{ax + b}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always rewrite roots as fractional powers and fractions as negative powers before differentiating
• The product and quotient rules are needed when two functions of $x$ are multiplied or divided
• The chain rule is needed when one function is inside another
• For sums and differences, differentiate each term separately

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up the order in the quotient rule. The formula is $\dfrac{vu' - uv'}{v^2}$, NOT $\dfrac{uv' - vu'}{v^2}$. A quick check: if $u$ is the numerator, the first term in the numerator should start with $v \cdot u'$.

notes.heading: Tangents, Normals, and Curve Analysis
notes.body:
The derivative tells us the gradient of a curve at any point. This lets us find equations of tangents and normals, and analyse the shape of curves.

📌 Tangent and Normal
At any point on a curve:
• The tangent is a straight line that touches the curve and has the same gradient
• The normal is perpendicular to the tangent

🔑 Equations
    Gradient of tangent at $x = a$: $m_T = f'(a)$
    Equation of tangent: $y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a)$
    Gradient of normal: $m_N = -\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}$ (provided $f'(a) 
eq 0$)
    Equation of normal: $y - f(a) = \left(-\dfrac{1}{f'(a)}\right)(x - a)$

💡 Worked Example — Tangent and Normal
Find the tangent and normal to $y = x^2$ at the point $(2, 4)$.

  Step 1: Find the derivative
    $$f'(x) = 2x$$

  Step 2: Gradient of tangent at $x = 2$
    $$m_T = f'(2) = 4$$

  Step 3: Equation of tangent
    $$y - 4 = 4(x - 2)$$
    $$y = 4x - 4$$

  Step 4: Gradient of normal
    $$m_N = -\dfrac{1}{4}$$

  Step 5: Equation of normal
    $$y - 4 = \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}\right)(x - 2)$$
    $$y = -\dfrac{1}{4}x + \dfrac{9}{2}$$

📌 Increasing and Decreasing Functions
• $f'(x) > 0$ → $f$ is increasing
• $f'(x) < 0$ → $f$ is decreasing

📌 Stationary Points
A stationary point occurs where $f'(x) = 0$. The tangent is horizontal.

🔑 First Derivative Test (sign change)
Check the sign of $f'(x)$ on either side of the stationary point:
• $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$ → local maximum
• $f'$ changes from $-$ to $+$ → local minimum
• $f'$ does not change sign → horizontal point of inflection

🔑 Second Derivative Test
Evaluate $f''(x)$ at the stationary point:
• $f''(c) < 0$ → concave down → local maximum
• $f''(c) > 0$ → concave up → local minimum
• $f''(c) = 0$ → test is inconclusive, use first derivative test

💡 Worked Example — Finding Stationary Points
Find the stationary points of $f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 36x + 25$ and determine their nature.

  Step 1: Find $f'(x)$ and solve $f'(x) = 0$
    $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 6x - 36$$
    $$6x^2 - 6x - 36 = 0$$
    $$x^2 - x - 6 = 0$$
    $$(x - 3)(x + 2) = 0$$
    $$x = 3 	ext{ or } x = -2$$

  Step 2: Find $y$-coordinates
    $$f(3) = 54 - 27 - 108 + 25 = -56$$
    $$f(-2) = -16 - 12 + 72 + 25 = 69$$
    Stationary points: $(3, -56)$ and $(-2, 69)$

  Step 3: Second derivative test
    $$f''(x) = 12x - 6$$
    $$f''(3) = 30 > 0$$
    → local minimum at $(3, -56)$
    $$f''(-2) = -30 < 0$$
    → local maximum at $(-2, 69)$

📌 Point of Inflection
A point of inflection is where the concavity changes.
    $$f''(x) = 0 	ext{ AND the sign of } f'' 	ext{ changes through the point}$$
A point of inflection does NOT have to be a stationary point.

💡 Worked Example — Point of Inflection
Show that $f(x) = x^3$ has a point of inflection at $(0, 0)$.

  Step 1: Find $f''(x)$
    $$f'(x) = 3x^2$$
    $$f''(x) = 6x$$

  Step 2: Solve $f''(x) = 0$
    $$6x = 0 \rightarrow x = 0$$

  Step 3: Check concavity on either side
    $$f''(-1) = -6 < 0$$
    → concave down
    $$f''(1) = 6 > 0$$
    → concave up
    Concavity changes → point of inflection at $(0, 0)$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $f'(x)$ tells us the gradient; $f''(x)$ tells us the concavity
• Always check the sign changes for inflection points — $f''(x) = 0$ alone is not enough
• When $f''(c) = 0$ at a stationary point, the second derivative test fails — use the first derivative test instead
• The normal gradient is the negative reciprocal of the tangent gradient

⚠️ Common Mistake
Concluding that $f''(x) = 0$ automatically means a point of inflection. It does NOT. You must check that $f''(x)$ changes sign. For example, $f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ but $(0, 0)$ is a local minimum, not an inflection point.

notes.heading: Optimisation Problems
notes.body:
Optimisation is the process of finding the maximum or minimum value of a quantity in a real-world situation.

📌 What is Optimisation?
Any problem that asks you to maximise or minimise a quantity can be solved using differentiation. Examples include maximising area, minimising cost, or finding the greatest height.

🔑 The Six-Step Method
1. Draw a clear diagram and label variables
2. Write the quantity $Q$ to be optimised as a formula
3. Use constraints to express $Q$ in terms of a single variable
4. State the domain of the variable
5. Find $\dfrac{dQ}{dx}$, set it equal to zero, and solve
6. Verify max/min using the second derivative test or sign diagram
7. Write the final answer in context

💡 Worked Example — Maximum Area
A rectangle has a fixed perimeter of $60$ cm. Find the dimensions that give maximum area.

  Step 1: Define variables
    Let width = $x$, then length = $30 - x$
    (since perimeter = $2x + 2(30 - x) = 60$)

  Step 2: Write area formula
    $$A = x(30 - x) = 30x - x^2$$

  Step 3: State domain
    $$0 < x < 30$$

  Step 4: Differentiate and solve
    $$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 30 - 2x$$
    $$30 - 2x = 0 \rightarrow x = 15$$

  Step 5: Verify maximum
    $$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = -2 < 0$$
    → confirms a maximum

  Step 6: Answer
    Width = $15$ cm, length = $15$ cm
    Maximum area = $15 	imes 15 = 225$ cm$^2$
    The rectangle is a square.

💡 Worked Example — Minimising Surface Area
An open-top box with square base has volume $500$ cm$^3$. Find the base side that minimises surface area.

  Step 1: Define variables
    Let base side = $x$ cm, height = $h$ cm

  Step 2: Use volume constraint
    $$x^2 h = 500 \rightarrow h = \dfrac{500}{x^2}$$

  Step 3: Write surface area formula
    $$A = x^2 + 4xh \quad (	ext{base} + 	ext{four sides})$$
    $$A = x^2 + 4x\left(\dfrac{500}{x^2}\right)$$
    $$A = x^2 + \dfrac{2000}{x}$$

  Step 4: Differentiate and solve
    $$\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 2x - \dfrac{2000}{x^2}$$
    $$2x - \dfrac{2000}{x^2} = 0$$
    $$2x^3 = 2000$$
    $$x^3 = 1000$$
    $$x = 10$$

  Step 5: Verify minimum
    $$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = 2 + \dfrac{4000}{x^3}$$
    At $x = 10$:
    $$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2} = 2 + 4 = 6 > 0$$
    → confirms a minimum

  Step 6: Answer
    The base side should be $10$ cm.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always express the quantity in terms of ONE variable before differentiating
• Check endpoints of the domain as well as stationary points
• The second derivative test is usually the quickest way to verify max/min
• Write your final answer in the context of the problem, with units

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to check that a stationary point is actually a maximum or minimum. Always verify with the second derivative or a sign diagram. Also, don't forget to check endpoints — the optimal value might occur at a boundary.

notes.heading: Related Rates of Change
notes.body:
Related rates problems connect how two quantities change using the chain rule. They appear in many real-world contexts.

📌 What are Related Rates?
When two quantities are linked by a formula and both change with respect to time, their rates of change are related through differentiation.

🔑 The Chain Rule Connection
If $V$ and $r$ are linked, then:
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dr} 	imes \dfrac{dr}{dt}$$
In general:
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = \dfrac{dy}{dx} 	imes \dfrac{dx}{dt}$$
If it is easier to find $\dfrac{dx}{dy}$, you can also use:
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = \dfrac{\dfrac{dx}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dy}}$$

💡 Worked Example — Expanding Balloon
A spherical balloon is inflated so its radius increases at $2$ cm/s. Find the rate of increase of volume when $r = 5$ cm.

  Step 1: Write the linking formula
    $$V = \dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3$$

  Step 2: Differentiate with respect to $r$
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dr} = 4\pi r^2$$

  Step 3: Apply the chain rule
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dr} 	imes \dfrac{dr}{dt}$$
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2 	imes 2$$
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 8\pi r^2$$

  Step 4: Substitute $r = 5$
    $$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 8\pi(25) = 200\pi 	ext{ cm}^3/	ext{s}$$

💡 Worked Example — Sliding Ladder
A $5$ m ladder rests against a wall. The bottom slides away at $10$ cm/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the bottom is $3$ m from the wall?

  Step 1: Set up the diagram and formula
    $$x^2 + y^2 = 25 \quad (	ext{Pythagoras})$$

  Step 2: Differentiate implicitly with respect to time $t$
    $$2x \cdot \dfrac{dx}{dt} + 2y \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0$$
    $$x \cdot \dfrac{dx}{dt} + y \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0$$

  Step 3: Find $y$ when $x = 3$
    $$9 + y^2 = 25 \rightarrow y = 4$$

  Step 4: Substitute known values
    $$3 \cdot (10) + 4 \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0$$
    $$30 + 4 \cdot \dfrac{dy}{dt} = 0$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -7.5 	ext{ cm/s}$$

  Step 5: Interpret
    The negative sign means $y$ is decreasing.
    The top is sliding down at $7.5$ cm/s.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Step 1: Write a formula linking the two quantities
• Step 2: Differentiate implicitly with respect to time (or the linking variable)
• Step 3: Substitute known rates and values
• Always include units in the final answer
• Do not substitute particular values before differentiating

⚠️ Common Mistake
Substituting values too early. You must differentiate the general equation first, then substitute the specific instant. If you substitute before differentiating, you incorrectly treat variables as constants and the derivative will be zero.

notes.heading: Standard Derivatives
notes.body:
There are several derivatives you should know by heart. These are the building blocks for more complicated functions.

📌 Definition — Standard Derivatives
For the basic functions used in DP Mathematics:
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x) = \cos x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x) = -\sin x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(	an x) = \sec^2 x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^x) = e^x$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\ln x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \quad x > 0$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(a^x) = a^x \ln a$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\log_a x) = \dfrac{1}{x \ln a}$$

🔑 Key Concept — Chain rule with standard derivatives
When the argument is not simply $x$, multiply by the derivative of the inner function.
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[\sin(u)] = \cos(u) \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{u}) = e^{u} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$$
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}[\ln(u)] = \dfrac{1}{u} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx}$$

💡 Worked Example — Combining chain rule and standard derivatives
Differentiate $y = \ln(5x^2 + 3)$.

  Let $u = 5x^2 + 3$, so $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 10x$.
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{u} \cdot \dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{10x}{5x^2 + 3}$$

💡 Worked Example — Exponential with a coefficient
Differentiate $y = e^{4x^3}$.

    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{4x^3} \cdot \dfrac{d}{dx}(4x^3)$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = e^{4x^3} \cdot 12x^2 = 12x^2 e^{4x^3}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)$ has a negative sign.
• $\ln x$ is only defined for $x > 0$.
• Always look for an inner function before applying a standard derivative.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin(3x)) = \cos(3x)$ and forgetting to multiply by $3$. The correct answer is $3\cos(3x)$.

notes.heading: Concavity and Points of Inflection
notes.body:
The second derivative tells us about the curvature of a graph, not just the nature of stationary points.

📌 Definition — Concavity
A function is:
• Concave up on an interval if $f''(x) > 0$ (shaped like a cup $\cup$)
• Concave down on an interval if $f''(x) < 0$ (shaped like a cap $\cap$)

🔑 Key Concept — Point of inflection
A point of inflection is where the concavity changes. Two conditions must be met:
1. $f''(x) = 0$ (or $f''$ is undefined)
2. The sign of $f''(x)$ changes through the point

A stationary point of inflection also satisfies $f'(x) = 0$. A non-stationary point of inflection does not.

💡 Worked Example — Finding a point of inflection
Find the point of inflection of $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 5$.

  Step 1: Find the first derivative
    $$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x$$

  Step 2: Find the second derivative
    $$f''(x) = 6x - 12$$

  Step 3: Solve $f''(x) = 0$
    $$6x - 12 = 0 \rightarrow x = 2$$

  Step 4: Check sign change
    For $x < 2$, $f''(x) < 0$ (concave down).
    For $x > 2$, $f''(x) > 0$ (concave up).

  Step 5: Find the $y$-coordinate
    $$f(2) = 8 - 24 + 5 = -11$$

  The point of inflection is $(2, -11)$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming $f''(x) = 0$ always means a point of inflection. You must confirm the sign of $f''$ changes. For example, $f(x) = x^4$ has $f''(0) = 0$ but $(0, 0)$ is a minimum, not an inflection point.

notes.heading: Implicit Differentiation
notes.body:
Sometimes $y$ is not given explicitly as a function of $x$. Implicit differentiation lets us find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ without solving for $y$.

📌 Definition — Implicit function
An equation such as $x^2 + y^2 = 25$ defines $y$ implicitly in terms of $x$. Differentiating both sides with respect to $x$ gives an equation involving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.

🔑 How it works
1. Differentiate every term with respect to $x$.
2. When differentiating a term in $y$, multiply by $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ (chain rule).
3. Collect terms containing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ on one side.
4. Factor out $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ and solve.

💡 Worked Example — Circle
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ for $x^2 + y^2 = 25$.

  Step 1: Differentiate both sides
    $$\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2) + \dfrac{d}{dx}(y^2) = \dfrac{d}{dx}(25)$$
    $$2x + 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$$

  Step 2: Solve for $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$
    $$2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -2x$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}$$

💡 Worked Example — Product needed
Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $x^3 + xy + y^2 = 7$.

  Step 1: Differentiate term by term
    $$3x^2 + \left(x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + y\right) + 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$$

  Step 2: Collect $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ terms
    $$x \dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -3x^2 - y$$

  Step 3: Factor and solve
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}(x + 2y) = -3x^2 - y$$
    $$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{3x^2 + y}{x + 2y}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to multiply by $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ when differentiating $y^2$. Treat $y$ as a function of $x$, so $\dfrac{d}{dx}(y^2) = 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx}$.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example — Harder Optimisation with Unequal Costs
notes.body:
This example combines optimisation with a real-world cost constraint where different parts of an object have different unit costs.

📌 Problem
A closed cylindrical can must hold exactly $1000$ cm$^3$. The material for the top and bottom circular ends costs twice as much per cm$^2$ as the material for the curved side. Find the radius and height that minimise the total material cost.

🔑 Strategy
1. Let the curved side cost $k$ per cm$^2$, so each circular end costs $2k$ per cm$^2$.
2. Write the total cost $C$ in terms of radius $r$ and height $h$.
3. Use the volume constraint to eliminate $h$.
4. Differentiate $C$ with respect to $r$, set to zero, and verify a minimum.

💡 Solution
  Step 1: Cost formula
    Area of curved side = $2\pi r h$
    Area of top and bottom together = $2\pi r^2$
    Total cost: $C = k(2\pi r h) + 2k(2\pi r^2) = 2\pi k r h + 4\pi k r^2$

  Step 2: Use the volume constraint
    $$V = \pi r^2 h = 1000 \rightarrow h = \dfrac{1000}{\pi r^2}$$

  Step 3: Express cost in one variable
    $$C = 2\pi k r \left(\dfrac{1000}{\pi r^2}\right) + 4\pi k r^2$$
    $$C = \dfrac{2000k}{r} + 4\pi k r^2$$

  Step 4: Differentiate with respect to $r$
    $$\dfrac{dC}{dr} = -\dfrac{2000k}{r^2} + 8\pi k r$$

  Step 5: Set derivative equal to zero
    $$-\dfrac{2000k}{r^2} + 8\pi k r = 0$$
    $$8\pi k r = \dfrac{2000k}{r^2}$$
    $$8\pi r^3 = 2000$$
    $$r^3 = \dfrac{250}{\pi}$$
    $$r = \sqrt[3]{\dfrac{250}{\pi}} \approx 4.30 	ext{ cm}$$

  Step 6: Find the height
    $$h = \dfrac{1000}{\pi r^2} = \dfrac{1000}{\pi} \left(\dfrac{\pi}{250}\right)^{2/3} = 2\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{250}{\pi}} = 2r$$

  Step 7: Verify minimum
    $$\dfrac{d^2C}{dr^2} = \dfrac{4000k}{r^3} + 8\pi k > 0 \quad 	ext{for } r > 0$$
    → confirms a minimum.

  The cheapest can has height equal to twice its radius, with $r \approx 4.30$ cm and $h \approx 8.60$ cm.

questions.stem: $\dfrac{d}{dx}[\ln(4x + 3)]$?
questions.explanation: Chain rule: derivative of $\ln(u)$ is $\dfrac{u'}{u}$. Here $u = 4x + 3$, so $u' = 4$. Answer = $\dfrac{4}{4x + 3}$.

questions.stem: An open-top box with square base has volume $500$ cm$^3$. Find the base side length that minimises surface area.
questions.explanation: Let base side = $x$ and height = $h$. Volume $x^2 h = 500$ → $h = \dfrac{500}{x^2}$. Surface area $A = x^2 + 4xh = x^2 + \dfrac{2000}{x}$. $\dfrac{dA}{dx} = 2x - \dfrac{2000}{x^2} = 0$ → $2x^3 = 2000$ → $x^3 = 1000$ → $x = 10$ cm. Second derivative is positive, confirming a minimum.

questions.stem: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin(3x))$?
questions.explanation: Chain rule: derivative of $\sin(3x)$ is $\cos(3x) 	imes 3 = 3\cos(3x)$.

questions.stem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point of inflection of $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 4$.
questions.explanation: $f''(x) = 6x - 12$. Setting $f''(x) = 0$ gives $x = 2$, and the sign of $f''$ changes through $x = 2$, so it is a point of inflection.

questions.stem: Given $x^2 + y^2 = 25$, find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.explanation: Implicit differentiation gives $2x + 2y \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{y}$.

questions.stem: A straight river is 2 km wide. An oil refinery is on one bank and a storage tank is 8 km downstream on the opposite bank. Pipe laid underwater costs 50 units per km, while pipe laid on land costs 30 units per km. The pipeline will cross the river at some point and then continue along the opposite bank to the tank. Find the distance downstream from the refinery at which the pipeline should reach the opposite bank to minimise cost.
questions.explanation: Let $x$ be the downstream distance on the opposite bank where the pipe reaches land. Underwater length is $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$ and land length is $8 - x$. Cost is $C = 50\sqrt{x^2 + 4} + 30(8 - x)$. Differentiating gives $\dfrac{dC}{dx} = \dfrac{50x}{\sqrt{x^2 + 4}} - 30$. Setting to zero yields $50x = 30\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$, so $25x^2 = 9(x^2 + 4)$ and $x = 1.5$ km. The second derivative is positive, confirming a minimum.

questions.stem: Find the gradient of the curve $x^3 + y^3 = 6xy$ at the point $(3, 3)$.
questions.explanation: Differentiating implicitly with respect to $x$ gives $3x^2 + 3y^2 \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6y + 6x \dfrac{dy}{dx}$. Collecting terms containing $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ yields $\dfrac{dy}{dx}(3y^2 - 6x) = 6y - 3x^2$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{6y - 3x^2}{3y^2 - 6x}$. Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = 3$ gives $\dfrac{18 - 27}{27 - 18} = \dfrac{-9}{9} = -1$.

questions.stem: A cone with vertex pointing downwards has base radius 4 m and height 8 m. Water is poured in at a constant rate of $5$ m$^3$/min. Find the rate at which the water level is rising when the depth of the water is $2$ m.
questions.explanation: By similar triangles, when the water depth is $h$ the radius of the water surface is $r = \dfrac{h}{2}$. The volume of water is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{\pi h^3}{12}$. Differentiating gives $\dfrac{dV}{dh} = \dfrac{\pi h^2}{4}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{dV}{dt} \div \dfrac{dV}{dh} = \dfrac{5}{\pi h^2/4} = \dfrac{20}{\pi h^2}$. Substituting $h = 2$ gives $\dfrac{20}{4\pi} = \dfrac{5}{\pi}$ m/min.

questions.stem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7$ at the point $(1, 2)$.
questions.explanation: Differentiating implicitly gives $2x + y + x\dfrac{dy}{dx} + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$. Collecting the derivative terms yields $\dfrac{dy}{dx}(x + 2y) = -2x - y$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$. At $(1, 2)$ the gradient is $-\dfrac{4}{5}$. Using $y - 2 = -\dfrac{4}{5}(x - 1)$ and rearranging gives $4x + 5y = 14$.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the curve $y = x^2$. Its $x$-coordinate increases at $3$ cm/s. Find the rate of change of the distance from the particle to the origin when $x = 2$.
questions.explanation: Let $D$ be the distance from the particle to the origin, so $D^2 = x^2 + y^2 = x^2 + x^4$. Differentiating implicitly with respect to time gives $2D\dfrac{dD}{dt} = (2x + 4x^3)\dfrac{dx}{dt}$. When $x = 2$, $y = 4$ and $D = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}$. Substituting $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3$ gives $\dfrac{dD}{dt} = \dfrac{(4 + 32)(3)}{2(2\sqrt{5})} = \dfrac{27}{\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{27\sqrt{5}}{5}$ cm/s.
